label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Dear Nana,

By the time Denise reads this to you, you’ll be sitting in the kitchen on Kathleen Street on your last night before the move. I wish more than anything that I could be sitting there with you. I tried to find someone to swap on-call shifts with me, but it just didn’t work out. I know you understand, and I know everyone keeps telling me it’s fine. I still hate missing it. Please don’t think for one second that my not being there means I don’t care about this day, or about everything that house has meant.

I’ve started this letter a bunch of times and kept stopping because I wanted to get it right. Fifty-one years is a lot to fit into an envelope. A card saying “Good luck with the move!” didn’t seem quite sufficient, so now Denise has to read you a small novel instead. Sorry, Denise.

When I think about that house, I think about summer first. I think about being a kid and getting to stay up to watch the Expos or the Jays on that little television in the kitchen, as long as I dried the dishes. At the time, I thought I’d negotiated an excellent deal. Looking back, I’m not sure who was getting the better end of it. You got the dishes dried and some company, and I got to stay up late and feel extremely grown up. It seemed so ordinary then. Now it’s one of those memories I can bring back just by thinking about the kitchen.

I think about the back steps too. You sitting there at six in the morning with your tea, and me coming out to join you. You never talked until you’d finished the cup. I don’t remember us having especially important conversations out there. Mostly I remember that I could come and sit down and be with you, and nobody had to fill the silence. Considering that my job now involves alarms going off because computers are unhappy, I probably should have spent more time appreciating your advanced mastery of peace and quiet.

And, of course, there was crib.

You taught me when I was about seven, and you never once let me win. Not once. There were no suddenly terrible decisions on your part, no pretending you hadn’t noticed fifteen-two just because I was little. You taught me the game, and then you beat me at it fairly for years. When I finally skunked you at fifteen, you made me an entire pan of butter tarts. That was very gracious of you, considering what I’d just done to your dignity.

I loved those tarts, but I think I understood even then that the win mattered because I’d earned it. You never made me feel small for losing. You just kept dealing me back in. That’s a pretty good thing to teach a kid, whether you meant to or not.

Now I hear Elmwood Terrace has a crib league. I feel the other residents should be given some warning before you arrive. Perhaps one quiet week to settle in and make friends, and then you can start playing properly. Between that and Tuesdays with the church ladies, your social schedule is getting out of hand.

You raised half the family in that kitchen. I don’t just mean the big things, either. I mean all the ordinary days, all the people who came through, all the talking and feeding and listening and sitting with somebody until they were ready to say what was actually wrong. You did an awful lot of life in that room. For me, Kathleen Street isn’t just an address. When somebody mentions it, I picture you.

Grandpa Walt is part of all those memories too. None of that gets packed into a box or left behind when you go. The years you had together there, and everything the family became in that house, are still yours. Moving doesn’t erase any of it.

I don’t want this to sound like a funeral for the house, especially when you’ve got a new place to look forward to. I just didn’t want the night to pass without telling you what it meant to me. It was one of the steadiest places in my life. Not because nothing ever changed there, but because you were there. That’s the part I’ll always carry around.

Some of my favourite proof of that has come in much smaller moments. When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card that said, “for pizza, you look thin on the computer.” That was financial assistance, career congratulations and a nutritional assessment all in one envelope. I’ve had a few official workplace messages since then. None have been nearly that useful.

Then last Christmas, my pager went off during dinner and you wanted to know if the internet was broken again and whether I’d fixed it. For the record, I do not personally fix the entire internet. I appreciate your confidence, though. And now, every time we talk, you ask, “Did anything break?” The honest answer is usually yes. Something somewhere is generally broken. That’s more or less why they pay me. I love that you ask. It always makes me laugh, even when the answer involves a long night ahead.

So yes, I’m sad not to be in that kitchen with you tonight. But I’m also proud of you, and I don’t want the sad part to crowd that out.

You’re eighty-eight, and you chose this move yourself. Nobody made you do it. You looked at what you wanted and picked Elmwood Terrace. I’m proud of you for making your own decision and for going into this with some excitement instead of treating it like the end of something. You’ve spent a lifetime handling whatever came next, and here you are doing it again.

By the looks of it, Elmwood is actually pretty nice. Your room is on the second floor, with the big maple outside. There’s also the parking lot, but if anyone asks about the view, I suggest leading with the maple and mentioning the parking lot only if pressed. Every good view needs somewhere for Denise to park anyway.

I hope it starts feeling like yours quickly. I hope you find your favourite place to sit, figure out who deals a decent game of crib, and get exactly as involved or uninvolved in things as you want. You don’t have to make the new apartment into Kathleen Street. It gets to be something different. You’re allowed to enjoy that.

I’m glad Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest. As for me, I meant what I said about the crib board. I think I’ve been extremely restrained. Please don’t let it end up at the bottom of a box marked “miscellaneous.” That board has a future, and its future is me trying to beat you without any assistance whatsoever.

I’ll be up the weekend of December 5, as soon as my rotation is done. I want to see your room, admire the maple, and hear everything about the new place. You can tell me who you’ve met, what’s good, what’s strange, and whether anybody at Elmwood has made the mistake of thinking you’re an easy opponent.

Then we’re getting out the crib board.

No letting me win, obviously. I wouldn’t respect either of us if you started now. And if I manage to skunk you again, I’m not saying you have to make butter tarts, but I am saying there’s a precedent.

So save me a seat and keep the crib board handy. On December 5, I want the first game with you at Elmwood Terrace.

I love you, Nana. I’ll see you soon.

Love,  
[Your name]
